title: India's Ashith Surya and Amrutha Pramuthesh Fall to Golden Point Heartbreak at BWF World Championships
excerpt: The reserve mixed doubles pair pushed Turkey to the brink in a 71-minute thriller at New Delhi's Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium before losing on badminton's rarely invoked 30-point cap rule.
body:
• India's Ashith Surya and Amrutha Pramuthesh lost 21-16, 29-30, 22-24 to Turkey's Emre Sonmez and Yasemen Bektas in the mixed doubles Round of 32 at the BWF World Championships in New Delhi.
  • The golden point rule — where the first side to 30 wins when the score reaches 29-all — decided the dramatic second game.
  • The Indian pair, ranked World No. 44, were late entrants who travelled 1,800 km to reach the tournament after being called up as reserves.
  • India's other doubles pair, Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand, made a strong start in the women's doubles draw on the same day.

A 71-Minute Thriller Ends in Heartbreak

Ashith Surya and Amrutha Pramuthesh's BWF World Championships debut will be remembered for its drama as much as its outcome. The Indian mixed doubles pair lost 21-16, 29-30, 22-24 to Turkey's Emre Sonmez and Yasemen Bektas on Tuesday at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium, falling victim to badminton's golden point rule in a match that lasted 71 exhausting minutes.

The Indians looked in command after taking the opening game 21-16. But the second game became a war of attrition, with neither side able to establish the two-point lead required to win after the score passed 20-all. At 29-29, the golden point rule kicked in — the next rally decides the game, no two-point margin needed. Turkey won that crucial rally to level the match at one game apiece, 30-29.

"A scoreline of 30-29 is not something badminton fans see every day."

— CricketNMore, reporting from the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium

The Golden Point Rule Explained

Badminton's scoring system requires a two-point advantage to win a game once the score reaches 20-all. However, the sport imposes a hard cap at 30 points. If the score reaches 29-29, the next point wins the game outright — no two-point lead is necessary. This is known as the golden point, and it transforms the final rally into a sudden-death moment that can swing an entire match.

For Ashith and Amrutha, losing at golden point proved psychologically devastating. Despite showing resilience in the decider and staying competitive at 22-24, the momentum had shifted irreversibly. Turkey closed out the match to advance, leaving the Indian pair to reflect on how close they came to a historic win.

From Reserves to the World Stage

The backstory makes the near-miss even more poignant. Ashith and Amrutha were not originally in the main draw. Called up as reserves, the pair reportedly made an 1,800-kilometre dash to reach New Delhi in time for their first-round match. Having recently climbed to World No. 44 in the mixed doubles rankings — a jump of 10 places — they were riding a wave of form that made their late inclusion feel less like charity and more like reward.

Their journey from domestic-level competition to a World Championships that India is hosting at the Indira Gandhi Arena underscores the depth emerging in Indian badminton's doubles programme. The pair had previously shown promise with a dominant win over Sri Lanka's Thulith Palliyaguru and Panchali Adhikari at the 2025 Badminton Asia Championships.

Other Indian Performances

India's campaign at the home World Championships extended well beyond the mixed doubles. Lakshya Sen, the country's top men's singles hope, overcame a poor first game to beat Austria's Collins Filimon 16-21, 21-8, 21-4 in the Round of 64, crediting a tactical shift and better understanding of court conditions for the turnaround. In women's doubles, Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand made a strong start to their campaign.

The BWF World Championships continue through August 23 at the Indira Gandhi Arena, with quarterfinals on August 20-21 and finals on August 23. India, as host nation, has its largest-ever contingent competing across all five disciplines.
